title: Matrix Function Reduction via Cayley-Hamilton
description: Any polynomial function of an n×n matrix A reduces to a polynomial of degree at most n-1: aeval A p = aeval A (p mod charpoly(A)). This enables efficient computation of matrix powers, exponentials, and other matrix functions.

overview.historicalContext:
The Cayley-Hamilton theorem (1858) states that every matrix satisfies its characteristic polynomial. A powerful corollary is that any polynomial function of an n×n matrix can be reduced to a polynomial of degree at most n-1. This reduction is the algebraic foundation for efficient computation of matrix exponentials, powers, and other matrix functions.

This principle is essential in control theory (computing e^{At} for linear systems dx/dt = Ax), signal processing, and numerical ODE solvers. Instead of computing A^100 directly, one reduces X^100 modulo charpoly(A) to get a polynomial of degree < n.
overview.problemStatement:
**Polynomial Reduction Theorem**: For any polynomial p and n×n matrix A:

aeval A p = aeval A (p mod charpoly(A))

where the remainder has degree < n. This means every polynomial function of A lies in the span {I, A, A^2, ..., A^{n-1}}.

**Power Reduction**: A^k = aeval A (X^k mod charpoly(A)) for all k.

**Matrix Exponential Foundation**: Finite partial sums of power series also reduce via charpoly, providing the algebraic basis for computing exp(tA) = c_0(t)I + c_1(t)A + ... + c_{n-1}(t)A^{n-1}.
overview.text: Any polynomial function of an n×n matrix A reduces to a polynomial of degree at most n-1: aeval A p = aeval A (p mod charpoly(A)). This enables efficient computation of matrix powers, exponentials, and other matrix functions.
overview.proofStrategy:
The proof uses the polynomial division algorithm for monic polynomials. Since charpoly(A) is monic, any polynomial p decomposes as p = q * charpoly(A) + r where deg(r) < n. Evaluating at A and using Cayley-Hamilton (aeval A charpoly(A) = 0) yields aeval A p = aeval A r.

The degree bound follows from Mathlib's degree_modByMonic_lt. Special cases for nilpotent matrices (charpoly = X^n implies A^n = 0) and idempotent matrices (A^k = A for k > 0) are derived as corollaries.
keyInsights: The characteristic polynomial acts as a modular reduction for matrix polynomial evaluation
Any polynomial expression in A reduces to one of degree < n, giving a finite-dimensional computation
Two polynomials with the same remainder mod charpoly evaluate to the same matrix
The annihilator of A forms an ideal containing charpoly (closure under + and left multiplication)
Partial sums of power series (like exp(tA)) also reduce, connecting to matrix exponentials
Nilpotent matrices have charpoly = X^n, so all powers >= n vanish

sections.title: The Polynomial Reduction Theorem
sections.summary: Core result: aeval A p = aeval A (p mod charpoly(A)). Uses division algorithm and Cayley-Hamilton annihilation.
sections.mathContext: For any polynomial $q(X)$, $q(A) = r(A)$ where $r = q \mod p_A$ and $\deg r < n$. This is because $p_A(A) = 0$ by Cayley-Hamilton, so $q(A) \equiv r(A) \pmod{p_A(A)}$.

sections.title: Degree Bounds
sections.summary: The reduced polynomial has degree < deg(charpoly) = n, bounding matrix expressions to the span of {I, A, ..., A^{n-1}}.
sections.mathContext: The reduced polynomial $r = q \mod p_A$ has $\deg r < \deg p_A = n$, so $q(A) = r_0 I + r_1 A + \cdots + r_{n-1} A^{n-1}$. The matrix algebra $R[A] \subseteq \text{Mat}_n(R)$ is spanned by $\{I, A, \ldots, A^{n-1}\}$.

sections.title: Power Reduction
sections.summary: Matrix powers A^k expressed as evaluation of X^k mod charpoly. Every power reduces to degree < n.
sections.mathContext: For any polynomial $q(X)$, $q(A) = r(A)$ where $r = q \mod p_A$ and $\deg r < n$. This is because $p_A(A) = 0$ by Cayley-Hamilton, so $q(A) \equiv r(A) \pmod{p_A(A)}$.

sections.title: Congruence and Algebraic Structure
sections.summary: Two polynomials congruent mod charpoly evaluate identically. The annihilator forms an ideal.
sections.mathContext: The quotient ring $R[X]/(p_A)$ is isomorphic to the algebra $R[A]$ generated by $A$. Two polynomials $q_1, q_2$ satisfy $q_1(A) = q_2(A)$ iff $p_A \mid (q_1 - q_2)$.

sections.title: Partial Sum Reduction
sections.summary: Finite partial sums of power series reduce via charpoly, providing the foundation for computing matrix exponentials.
sections.mathContext: For the matrix exponential: $\sum_{k=0}^{N} \frac{(At)^k}{k!} = \sum_{j=0}^{n-1} \left(\sum_{k=0}^{N} \frac{t^k}{k!} [X^k \mod p_A]_j\right) A^j$ where $[\cdot]_j$ denotes the $j$-th coefficient of the reduced polynomial.

sections.title: Special Cases
sections.summary: Nilpotent matrices (A^n = 0 from charpoly = X^n), idempotent matrices (A^k = A), and concrete 2x2 examples.
sections.mathContext: Nilpotent: $p_N = \lambda^n$, so $N^n = 0$ and $e^{Nt} = \sum_{k=0}^{n-1} \frac{(Nt)^k}{k!}$ (exact finite sum). Idempotent: $P^2 = P$ gives $P^k = P$ for $k \geq 1$, and $e^{Pt} = I + (e^t-1)P$.

conclusion.summary: This formalization proves the polynomial reduction theorem: any polynomial function of an n×n matrix A equals the evaluation of its remainder modulo the characteristic polynomial. All 17 theorems are fully proved (0 sorries), establishing the algebraic foundation for matrix function computation.
conclusion.implications:
**Control Theory**: The matrix exponential exp(tA) reduces to n coefficients, enabling efficient computation of linear system responses.

**Numerical Methods**: Instead of computing A^k by repeated multiplication, reduce X^k mod charpoly to a low-degree polynomial.

**Signal Processing**: Transfer functions and z-transforms of matrix systems simplify via this reduction.

**Abstract Algebra**: The evaluation map factors through R[X]/(charpoly), an n-dimensional quotient ring.
openQuestions: Can this reduction be made computationally efficient for sparse matrices?
How does the minimal polynomial give a tighter reduction than the characteristic polynomial?
What is the analog for infinite-dimensional operators (compact operators on Hilbert spaces)?

crossReferences.description: Parent proof: the Cayley-Hamilton theorem (a matrix satisfies its own characteristic polynomial) — this file shows how to reduce matrix functions modulo the characteristic polynomial
The minimal polynomial approach to Cayley-Hamilton — this file uses the characteristic polynomial directly for matrix function reduction
Cramer's rule uses determinants of matrices; the characteristic polynomial involves det(A - λI), connecting determinant theory to eigenvalue analysis
Matrix power expansion and polynomial evaluation at matrices use binomial-type identities for the algebraic manipulations

Over $\mathbb{C}$ the characteristic polynomial splits completely by the fundamental theorem of algebra, so the reduction mod $\text{charpoly}(A)$ can be computed via partial fractions from eigenvalues

Lagrange's theorem (subgroup order divides group order) is the algebraic analogue of the minimal polynomial dividing the characteristic polynomial — both reflect quotient structure in their respective settings
De Moivre's formula computes powers of rotation matrices via $e^{in\theta}$; the Cayley-Hamilton reduction reduces these matrix powers to linear combinations of $I$ and $A$ for $2 \times 2$ rotations

The characteristic polynomial of a matrix determines a field extension via its splitting field; the Galois group of this extension governs the algebraic structure of the matrix's eigenvalues and Jordan form
